cards.front: How is Indian secularism different from the Western model? When was ‘secular’ added to the Preamble, and which case made secularism part of the basic structure?
cards.back:
• Western model (USA/France): a strict wall of separation – the State keeps out of religion.
  • Indian model: positive secularism – equal respect for all religions and ‘principled distance’. The State can still reform religious practices (e.g. Art. 17, temple-entry laws).
  • Added: by the 42nd Amendment, 1976.
  • Basic structure: S.R. Bommai (1994).
  • Related: Art. 27 – no one can be forced to pay taxes used to promote a particular religion.

⚠ Common mistake: Treating Indian secularism as the American/French ‘wall of separation’. India’s model is equal respect, not non-involvement.

cards.front: Write out the forms of Justice, Liberty and Equality as stated in the Preamble. From where were these ideals borrowed?
cards.back:
IdealForms in the PreambleSource
JusticeSocial, economic and politicalRussian Revolution (1917)
LibertyOf thought, expression, belief, faith and worshipFrench Revolution (1789)
EqualityOf status and of opportunityFrench Revolution
FraternityAssuring the dignity of the individual and the unity and integrity of the NationFrench Revolution

⚠ Common mistake: Writing ‘economic liberty’. The word ‘economic’ goes only with justice; the Preamble has no economic liberty.

cards.front:
Who chaired these committees of the Constituent Assembly?

  1. Union Powers Committee
  2. Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights, Minorities and Tribal & Excluded Areas
  3. Steering Committee
  4. Drafting Committee
cards.back:
1. Jawaharlal Nehru (he also chaired the Union Constitution and States Committees)
  2. Sardar Patel (he also chaired the Provincial Constitution Committee)
  3. Dr. Rajendra Prasad (also the Rules of Procedure Committee)
  4. Dr. B.R. Ambedkar

⚠ Common mistake: Giving the Advisory Committee to Nehru or the Steering Committee to Ambedkar. Hook: Nehru – Union; Patel – Provinces & Advisory; Prasad – Steering.

cards.front:
Answer the following about the enactment and enforcement of the Constitution:

  1. Which provisions came into force on 26 November 1949?
  2. Why was 26 January chosen as the date of commencement?
  3. On what date were the National Anthem and National Song adopted?
cards.back:
1. Provisions on citizenship, elections, provisional Parliament, temporary and transitional provisions and the short title (Arts. 5–9, 60, 324, 366, 367, 379, 380, 388, 391–394).
  2. 26 January 1930 had been celebrated as Purna Swaraj Day, following the Lahore Session (Dec 1929).
  3. 24 January 1950 – the final session, when members signed the Constitution and elected Rajendra Prasad as President.

⚠ Common mistake: Thinking the whole Constitution started on 26 January 1950, or that the Anthem was adopted on 26 November 1949.

cards.front:
From which country was each of these features borrowed?

  1. Residuary powers with the Centre
  2. Suspension of Fundamental Rights during Emergency
  3. Procedure established by law
  4. Due process / judicial review
  5. Nomination of members to the Rajya Sabha
cards.back:
1. Canada
  2. Weimar Constitution (Germany)
  3. Japan
  4. USA (judicial review; India did not adopt ‘due process’ in Art. 21)
  5. Ireland (also DPSPs and the method of electing the President)

⚠ Common mistake: Attributing ‘procedure established by law’ to the USA. The USA gave ‘due process’; Japan gave ‘procedure established by law’.

cards.front:
Answer the following about the text of the Preamble:

  1. Which date does the Preamble mention, and for what?
  2. What does fraternity assure?
  3. What kind of socialism does ‘socialist’ mean?
cards.back:
1. 26 November 1949 – the date of adoption (“…this twenty-sixth day of November, 1949, do hereby adopt, enact and give to ourselves this Constitution”).
  2. The dignity of the individual and the unity and integrity of the Nation (‘integrity’ added in 1976).
  3. Democratic socialism – a mixed economy, not Marxist socialism that abolishes private property.

⚠ Common mistake: Thinking the Preamble mentions 26 January 1950. It mentions only the date of adoption.

cards.front:
Classify these by the majority needed to amend them:

  1. Representation of States in Parliament
  2. Fundamental Rights
  3. GST Council
  4. Formation of new States
  5. Election of the President
cards.back:
Majority neededProvisions
Special majority + ratification by half the StatesRepresentation of States in Parliament; GST Council (101st Amendment, 2016); election of the President
Special majority onlyFundamental Rights
Simple majority (outside Art. 368)Formation of new States (Arts. 2–4)

⚠ Common mistake: Assuming anything that affects States needs ratification. Forming new States needs only a simple majority; only the federal provisions listed in Art. 368(2) need ratification.

cards.front: Can Parliament cede Indian territory to a foreign country under Article 3? How was the land exchange with Bangladesh carried out?
cards.back:
• Art. 3: No. Berubari Union (1960) – ceding territory needs a constitutional amendment under Art. 368. (Settling a boundary dispute does not.)
  • Bangladesh: the 100th Amendment Act, 2015 gave effect to the Land Boundary Agreement – India transferred 111 enclaves and received 51.

⚠ Common mistake: Thinking Art. 3 covers ceding territory abroad. It covers reorganisation within India only.

cards.front:
Answer the following about Article 32:

  1. Is the right to move the Supreme Court itself a Fundamental Right?
  2. Can other courts be given writ powers?
  3. Can the right to enforce Arts. 20 and 21 be suspended in an emergency?
cards.back:
1. Yes – Ambedkar called it the ‘heart and soul’ of the Constitution.
  2. Yes – under Art. 32(3) Parliament can empower any other court to issue writs within its local limits (no such law yet).
  3. No – since the 44th Amendment (1978), Arts. 20 and 21 cannot be suspended under Art. 359.

⚠ Common mistake: Forgetting the 44th Amendment safeguard for Arts. 20 and 21.

cards.front: What do Articles 33 and 34 provide? Is martial law defined in the Constitution?
cards.back:
• Art. 33: only Parliament (not State Legislatures) can restrict FRs of the armed forces, paramilitary forces, police, intelligence agencies and their telecom staff.
  • Art. 34: Parliament can indemnify any person for acts done to maintain or restore order where martial law was in force; the Indemnity Act cannot be challenged for violating FRs.
  • Martial law: not defined anywhere in the Constitution.

⚠ Common mistake: Treating martial law like a National Emergency. It is undefined and local.

cards.front: Which Fundamental Rights are available only to citizens? Are Arts. 21A and 25 available to foreigners?
cards.back:
• Citizens only: Arts. 15, 16, 19, 29 and 30.
  • Art. 21A: yes – all children aged 6–14.
  • Art. 25: yes – all persons.

⚠ Common mistake: Assuming minority rights (Arts. 29, 30) extend to foreigners.

cards.front: How does the Constitution deal with the education of children as a Fundamental Right, a Directive Principle and a Fundamental Duty? Give the Article, the age group and who is responsible under each.
cards.back:
CategoryArticleWhat it says
Fundamental RightArt. 21AThe State shall provide free and compulsory education to all children aged 6–14, in the manner the State may by law decide (RTE Act, 2009)
Directive PrincipleArt. 45The State shall endeavour to provide early childhood care and education for all children until they complete six years
Fundamental DutyArt. 51A(k)A parent or guardian shall provide opportunities for education to their child or ward aged 6–14

All three were brought in by the 86th Amendment Act, 2002. Before it, Art. 45 directed free and compulsory education for children up to 14.

⚠ Common mistake: Thinking Art. 45 still covers 6–14 education, or that the Art. 51A(k) duty is on the State. The duty is on parents/guardians; the State’s obligation is the FR under Art. 21A.

cards.front:
[UPSC CSE Prelims 2026] ‘X’ was addressing a seminar on the meaning of the term ‘law’ as provided under Article 13, Part III of the Constitution of India. X explained that the meaning of the term ‘law’ in the Constitution of India was very comprehensive. It included ordinances, orders and even rules and regulations. ‘Y’ pointed out that the term ‘law’ in Article 13 also included custom or usage having in the territory of India the force of law, to which ‘X’ was not convinced.

Based on the above, select the correct conclusion from the options given below:

(a) ‘X’ is correct in the interpretation of law, including the view on non-inclusion of custom
(b) The view of ‘Y’ that ‘law’ included custom is not correct
(c) The views of both ‘X’ and ‘Y’ are correct
(d) The view of only ‘Y’ is correct
cards.back:
Correct Answer: (d) The view of only ‘Y’ is correct

Article 13(3)(a) defines ‘law’ to include any ordinance, order, bye-law, rule, regulation, notification, custom or usage having in the territory of India the force of law.

⚠ Common mistake: Treating X as ‘partly right’. X’s view excludes custom, which contradicts Art. 13(3)(a), so only Y is correct.
